THOUGHT: This 9-month-old infant presents with a classic triad: (1) high fever (40.5°C) lasting ~3–5 days, (2) a febrile seizure (generalized tonic-clonic, brief, post-ictal recovery unremarkable), and (3) a generalized, nonpruritic, blanching maculopapular rash that appears *after* defervescence — starting on the trunk and spreading to extremities, with associated posterior auricular lymphadenopathy. The rash is nonpruritic and appears precisely 2 days after the fever broke — consistent with the typical timing of roseola (exanthem subitum). The patient is immunocompetent, fully vaccinated, and has normal CBC and electrolytes — making serious bacterial infection or vaccine-related reaction unlikely. The age (6–24 months), clinical course (fever → seizure → rash after defervescence), and physical findings (postauricular/occipital lymphadenopathy, blanching rash) strongly favor human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) or less commonly HHV-7 infection. Other considerations — such as measles — are highly unlikely given up-to-date immunizations (MMR not yet due at 9 months, but measles is rare in vaccinated populations and would present with cough/coryza/conjunctivitis/Koplik spots and *prodromal* illness before rash); scarlet fever would have pharyngitis, sandpaper rash, and likely elevated WBC/streptococcal markers; drug eruption is improbable with only acetaminophen (and rash would be less stereotyped); meningococcemia would show petechiae/purpura, toxicity, and lab abnormalities. The absence of systemic toxicity now (afebrile, well-appearing, normal vitals except mild tachycardia likely residual), and the characteristic lymphadenopathy, further support roseola.

DIAGNOSIS: Roseola infantum
